statement: Let $L$ be a [complete lattice](c:complete-lattice) and let $f\colon L \to L$ be a [monotone function](c:monotone-function). Then the set $\mathrm{Fix}(f)$ of [fixed points](c:fixed-point) of $f$, with the order of $L$, is a complete lattice; in particular $f$ has a least and a greatest fixed point.

hypotheses.text: The [partial order](c:partial-order) $L$ is a complete lattice: every subset has a [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) and an infimum.
The map $f$ is monotone: $x \le y$ implies $f(x) \le f(y)$.

conclusion: Every subset of $\mathrm{Fix}(f)$ has a supremum and an infimum inside $\mathrm{Fix}(f)$, so $\mathrm{Fix}(f)$ is a nonempty complete lattice.

proofs.name: Infimum of the pre-fixed points
proofs.slogan: The infimum of all points with $f(x) \le x$ is the least fixed point, and the same argument on an upper interval gives every join.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the empty subset gives the least and the greatest fixed point. Meets follow from joins by order duality.

roles.why: Completeness supplies the infimum of the pre-fixed points and makes each upper interval $[w, \top]$ a complete lattice.
Monotonicity turns $a \le x$ into $f(a) \le f(x)$ and keeps upper intervals invariant.

steps.slogan: Show that the infimum $a$ of $P = \{x : f(x) \le x\}$ is the least fixed point.
steps.detail: For $x \in P$, $a \le x$ gives $f(a) \le f(x) \le x$, so $f(a)$ is a lower bound of $P$ and $f(a) \le a$. Then $f(f(a)) \le f(a)$ puts $f(a)$ in $P$, so $a \le f(a)$ and $f(a) = a$. Every [fixed point](c:fixed-point) lies in $P$, so $a$ is below all of them.

steps.slogan: Restrict $f$ to the upper interval above the join $w$ of a set $W$ of fixed points.
steps.detail: Let $w = \sup W$ in $L$. For $x \ge w$ and $y \in W$, $f(x) \ge f(y) = y$, so $f(x) \ge w$. Hence $f$ maps $[w, \top]$, itself a [complete lattice](c:complete-lattice), monotonically into itself.

steps.slogan: Take the least fixed point $v$ of $f$ on $[w, \top]$ as the join of $W$ in $\mathrm{Fix}(f)$.
steps.detail: Step 1 on $[w, \top]$ gives a least fixed point $v \ge w$, an upper bound of $W$ in $\mathrm{Fix}(f)$. Any fixed upper bound $u$ of $W$ satisfies $u \ge w$, so $v \le u$. For $W = \emptyset$, $v$ is the least fixed point of $f$.

steps.slogan: Dualize the argument to get the meet of every set of fixed points.
steps.detail: The order dual of $L$ is a complete lattice and $f$ is monotone for it, so steps 1 to 3 in the dual order give the meet of $W$ in $\mathrm{Fix}(f)$. With all joins and meets, $\mathrm{Fix}(f)$ is a complete lattice, and it is nonempty.

concepts.c:complete-lattice: Completeness gives the infimum of pre-fixed points and complete upper intervals.
concepts.c:monotone-function: Monotonicity moves inequalities through $f$ and keeps intervals invariant.
concepts.c:fixed-point: The proof finds least fixed points as infima of pre-fixed points.
concepts.c:partial-order: The fixed points carry the order inherited from $L$.
concepts.c:least-upper-bound: Joins of fixed points start from their supremum in $L$.

source.note: Tarski's proof, A. Tarski, A lattice-theoretical fixpoint theorem and its applications, Pacific J. Math. 5 (1955); mathlib has it as OrderHom.lfp and fixedPoints.completeLattice.

statement: For each finite set $J$ of indices in a set $T$, let $\mu_J$ be a Borel [probability measure](c:probability-measure) on $\mathbb{R}^J$, and let the family be consistent under the coordinate projections. Then a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^T$ with the product $\sigma$-algebra has the $\mu_J$ as its [finite-dimensional distributions](c:finite-dimensional-distribution).

hypotheses.text: Each $\mu_J$, for finite $J \subseteq T$, is a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb{R}^J$.
The family is consistent: $\mu_J(\pi_{JI}^{-1}(B)) = \mu_I(B)$ for finite $I \subseteq J$ and Borel $B \subseteq \mathbb{R}^I$.

conclusion: A unique probability measure $\mu$ on $(\mathbb{R}^T, \mathcal{B}^T)$ satisfies $\mu \circ \pi_J^{-1} = \mu_J$ for every finite $J$, so the coordinates form a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) with these laws.

proofs.name: Cylinder premeasure and compact regularity
proofs.slogan: Define $\mu$ on cylinder sets, prove countable additivity there by compact inner approximation, and extend by Carathéodory's theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for real coordinates; the same proof works for Polish coordinate spaces. Uniqueness comes from the π-system of cylinders.

roles.why: Borel probability measures on $\mathbb{R}^J$ have total mass one and are inner regular by compact sets.
Consistency makes the value of a cylinder independent of its description, so the premeasure is well defined.

steps.slogan: Define $\mu_0(\pi_J^{-1}(B)) = \mu_J(B)$ on the algebra of cylinder sets.
steps.detail: Cylinder sets $\pi_J^{-1}(B)$, with $J$ finite and $B$ Borel, form an [algebra of sets](c:algebra-of-sets) that generates $\mathcal{B}^T$. Two descriptions of one cylinder can be written over a common finite $J$, where consistency gives them the same value, and finite additivity of $\mu_0$ follows from that of $\mu_J$.

steps.slogan: Approximate each cylinder base from inside by a compact set.
steps.detail: A Borel probability measure on $\mathbb{R}^J$ is [inner regular](c:inner-regular): for Borel $B$ and $\delta > 0$ some compact $K \subseteq B$ has $\mu_J(B \setminus K) < \delta$.

steps.slogan: Show that decreasing cylinders $C_n$ with $\mu_0(C_n) \ge \varepsilon$ have a common point.
steps.detail: Write $C_n = \pi_{J_n}^{-1}(B_n)$, pick compact $K_n \subseteq B_n$ with $\mu_{J_n}(B_n \setminus K_n) < \varepsilon 2^{-n-1}$, and let $D_n = \bigcap_{k \le n} \pi_{J_k}^{-1}(K_k) \subseteq C_n$; then $\mu_0(D_n) \ge \varepsilon/2$, so $D_n \ne \emptyset$. Points $x^n \in D_n$ have coordinates in compact sets, so a diagonal [subsequence](c:subsequence) converges coordinatewise to a point of every $D_n$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\mu_0$ is countably additive on the cylinder algebra.
steps.detail: Step 3 shows that $C_n \downarrow \emptyset$ forces $\mu_0(C_n) \to 0$. For a finite, finitely additive set function on an algebra, this continuity at $\emptyset$ gives countable additivity, so $\mu_0$ is a [pre-measure](c:pre-measure).

steps.slogan: Extend $\mu_0$ to the product $\sigma$-algebra and prove uniqueness on the cylinders.
steps.detail: Carathéodory's extension theorem extends $\mu_0$ to a probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal{B}^T$ with $\mu \circ \pi_J^{-1} = \mu_J$. Cylinders form a [π-system](c:pi-system) that generates $\mathcal{B}^T$, so Dynkin's theorem shows that two such measures agree.

concepts.c:probability-measure: Each $\mu_J$ is a probability measure, and so is the extension.
concepts.c:finite-dimensional-distribution: The extension must have the given finite-dimensional distributions.
concepts.c:stochastic-process: The coordinate maps under $\mu$ form the required process.
concepts.c:algebra-of-sets: Cylinder sets form the algebra on which the premeasure lives.
concepts.c:inner-regular: Compact inner approximation drives the continuity at the empty set.
concepts.c:subsequence: A diagonal subsequence produces a point in every compact cylinder.
concepts.c:pre-measure: Countable additivity on cylinders is what Carathéodory extension needs.
concepts.c:pi-system: Cylinders are closed under intersection, which gives uniqueness.

source.note: The standard proof by compact inner regularity and Carathéodory extension, as in Billingsley, Probability and Measure, section 36.

statement: Let $\alpha$ be a finite nonempty alphabet with $D$ letters and let $S$ be a [prefix code](c:prefix-code) over $\alpha$, finite or infinite: no word of $S$ is a proper prefix of another. Then the [word lengths](c:word-length) satisfy $\sum_{w \in S} D^{-|w|} \le 1$.

hypotheses.text: The alphabet $\alpha$ is finite and nonempty, with $D \ge 1$ letters.
The set $S$ of words over $\alpha$ is prefix-free.

conclusion: The Kraft sum $\sum_{w \in S} D^{-|w|}$ converges and is at most $1$.

proofs.name: Kraft-McMillan on finite parts
proofs.slogan: Bound every finite part of the code by the Kraft-McMillan counting argument, then pass to the sum over the whole code.
proofs.scope: Any prefix-free set, finite or infinite. The code $\{\varepsilon\}$ that holds the empty word is treated separately; its Kraft sum is exactly $1$.

roles.why: A finite alphabet bounds the number of words of length $s$ by $D^s$, and $D \ge 1$ makes $D^{-|w|}$ defined.
Prefix-freeness makes the code uniquely decodable and passes to every subset.

steps.slogan: Treat the case where the empty word belongs to $S$.
steps.detail: The empty word is a prefix of every word, so prefix-freeness forces $S = \{\varepsilon\}$, whose Kraft sum is $D^0 = 1$. From now on $\varepsilon \notin S$.

steps.slogan: Show that a prefix-free set without the empty word is a [uniquely decodable code](c:uniquely-decodable-code).
steps.detail: Read a concatenation of codewords from the left: only one codeword can be a prefix of it, since two such codewords would be prefixes of each other. Remove it and repeat, so each concatenation has a single factorization.

steps.slogan: Bound the $r$-th power of a finite Kraft sum by counting concatenations.
steps.detail: For a finite uniquely decodable $F$ with longest length $\ell$, $\big(\sum_{w \in F} D^{-|w|}\big)^r = \sum_{s \le r\ell} N_s D^{-s}$, where $N_s$ counts $r$-fold concatenations of length $s$. They are distinct [words](c:word), so $N_s \le D^s$ and the power is at most $r\ell$; taking $r$-th roots and $r \to \infty$ gives a sum at most $1$.

steps.slogan: Bound the Kraft sum of every finite subset of $S$ by $1$.
steps.detail: Every finite subset $F \subseteq S$ is again prefix-free, so steps 1 to 3 give $\sum_{w \in F} D^{-|w|} \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Pass from the finite partial sums to the sum over all of $S$.
steps.detail: The terms $D^{-|w|}$ are nonnegative and all finite partial sums are at most $1$, so the family is summable and its sum, the supremum of the partial sums, is at most $1$.

concepts.c:prefix-code: Prefix-freeness gives unique decoding and passes to subsets.
concepts.c:word-length: The Kraft sum weighs each codeword by its length.
concepts.c:uniquely-decodable-code: Unique decoding makes the counted concatenations distinct.
concepts.c:word: Concatenations of length $s$ are words, at most $D^s$ of them.

proofs.name: Disjoint D-adic intervals
proofs.slogan: Send each codeword to a $D$-adic subinterval of $[0, 1)$ of length $D^{-|w|}$; prefix-freeness makes these intervals disjoint.
proofs.scope: Any prefix-free set; for $D = 1$ the argument still works, since such a set has at most one word.

roles.why: With $D$ letters, words of length $k$ cut $[0, 1)$ into $D^k$ intervals of length $D^{-k}$.
Prefix-freeness makes the intervals of different codewords disjoint.

steps.slogan: Assign to each codeword a $D$-adic interval of length $D^{-|w|}$.
steps.detail: Number the letters $0, \dots, D-1$ and send $w = w_1 \cdots w_k$ to the [interval](c:interval) $I_w = [x_w, x_w + D^{-k})$ with $x_w = \sum_{i \le k} w_i D^{-i}$. Then $I_w \subseteq [0, 1)$ has length $D^{-|w|}$.

steps.slogan: Show that the intervals of two different codewords do not meet.
steps.detail: $D$-adic intervals are nested or disjoint, so if $I_v \cap I_w \ne \emptyset$ with $|v| \le |w|$, then $I_w \subseteq I_v$ and the first $|v|$ letters of $w$ form $v$. So $v$ is a prefix of $w$, and prefix-freeness gives $v = w$.

steps.slogan: Add the lengths of the disjoint intervals inside $[0, 1)$.
steps.detail: For finite $F \subseteq S$ the intervals $I_w$, $w \in F$, are disjoint subsets of $[0, 1)$, so $\sum_{w \in F} D^{-|w|} \le 1$. The supremum over finite $F$ gives the bound for the whole sum.

concepts.c:prefix-code: Prefix-freeness is exactly disjointness of the codeword intervals.
concepts.c:word-length: A word of length $k$ gets an interval of length $D^{-k}$.
concepts.c:interval: Disjoint subintervals of $[0, 1)$ have total length at most $1$.

source.note: The interval proof of Kraft's inequality, as in Cover and Thomas, Elements of Information Theory, chapter 5.

statement: Let $0 \le r < R \le \infty$ and let $f$ be [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the [annulus](c:annulus) $A = \{r < |z - c| < R\}$. Then $f(z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a_n (z - c)^n$ on $A$, with $a_n = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|w - c| = \rho} \frac{f(w)}{(w - c)^{n+1}}\,dw$ for any $\rho \in (r, R)$; the series converges absolutely and locally uniformly, and its coefficients are unique.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is holomorphic on the annulus $A = \{r < |z - c| < R\}$.
The radii satisfy $0 \le r < R \le \infty$.

conclusion: $f$ equals its [Laurent series](c:laurent-series) on $A$, and no other coefficients give such an expansion.

proofs.name: Cauchy formula on two circles
proofs.slogan: Write $f(z)$ as a difference of Cauchy integrals over an outer and an inner circle, and expand each kernel in a geometric series.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, including $r = 0$ (a punctured disk) and $R = \infty$. The outer circle gives the powers $n \ge 0$ and the inner circle the powers $n < 0$.

roles.why: Holomorphy on $A$ gives Cauchy's theorem between circles, hence the two-circle formula and radius-free coefficients.
The condition $r < R$ leaves room for circles of radii $\rho_1 < |z - c| < \rho_2$ inside $A$.

steps.slogan: Represent $f(z)$ by Cauchy integrals over two circles in the annulus.
steps.detail: Take $r < \rho_1 < |z - c| < \rho_2 < R$. The function $g(w) = (f(w) - f(z))/(w - z)$, with $g(z) = f'(z)$, is holomorphic on $A$, so its [contour integrals](c:contour-integral) over the two homotopic circles agree; this gives $f(z) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\rho_2} \frac{f(w)}{w - z}\,dw - \frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\rho_1} \frac{f(w)}{w - z}\,dw$.

steps.slogan: Expand $1/(w - z)$ on the outer circle in powers of $z - c$.
steps.detail: For $|w - c| = \rho_2 > |z - c|$, $\frac{1}{w - z} = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{(z - c)^n}{(w - c)^{n+1}}$ is a [geometric series](c:geometric-series) that converges [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) in $w$. Integration term by term gives $\sum_{n \ge 0} a_n (z - c)^n$.

steps.slogan: Expand $-1/(w - z)$ on the inner circle in powers of $1/(z - c)$.
steps.detail: For $|w - c| = \rho_1 < |z - c|$, $-\frac{1}{w - z} = \sum_{m \ge 1} \frac{(w - c)^{m-1}}{(z - c)^m}$, again uniformly in $w$. Integration term by term gives $\sum_{n \le -1} a_n (z - c)^n$ with $a_n$ the stated integral over the circle of radius $\rho_1$.

steps.slogan: Show that each coefficient integral does not depend on the radius $\rho$.
steps.detail: The integrand $f(w)(w - c)^{-n-1}$ is holomorphic on $A$ and any two circles about $c$ in $A$ are homotopic there, so Cauchy's theorem gives one $a_n$ for every $\rho \in (r, R)$. Comparison with geometric series gives absolute and locally uniform convergence.

steps.slogan: Integrate any such expansion against $(z - c)^{-k-1}$ to recover its coefficients.
steps.detail: A series $\sum b_n (z - c)^n$ that converges on $A$ converges uniformly on each circle $|z - c| = \rho$, so termwise integration with $\oint (z - c)^m\,dz = 2\pi i$ for $m = -1$ and $0$ otherwise gives $b_k = a_k$.

steps.slogan: Add the two expansions to get the Laurent series of $f$ with unique coefficients.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 4 give $f(z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} a_n (z - c)^n$ for every $z \in A$, with $a_n$ independent of $\rho$. Step 5 shows that no other coefficients represent $f$.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy makes Cauchy's theorem hold between the two circles.
concepts.c:annulus: The annulus holds both circles and the point $z$ between them.
concepts.c:laurent-series: The two expansions together form the Laurent series of $f$.
concepts.c:contour-integral: Coefficients and the two-circle formula are contour integrals.
concepts.c:geometric-series: Both Cauchy kernels expand as geometric series on their circles.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Uniform convergence on circles allows termwise integration.

source.note: The classical proof by the Cauchy integral formula on two circles, as in Ahlfors, Complex Analysis, chapter 5, section 1.3.

statement: Let $A, B, C$ be points of a [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space), the vertices of a possibly degenerate [triangle](c:triangle), with side lengths $a = |BC|$, $b = |CA|$, $c = |AB|$ and [angle](c:angle) $\gamma = \angle ACB$. Then $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos\gamma$.

hypotheses.text: The points lie in a Euclidean space: a real [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) with distance $|PQ| = \|P - Q\|$.

conclusion: The side opposite $C$ satisfies $c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos\gamma$, with the [cosine](c:cosine) of the angle at $C$.

formal.difference: The declaration holds for three points of any real inner product affine space, possibly infinite dimensional, and writes each square as a product of distances.

proofs.name: Expansion of a vector norm
proofs.slogan: Write the sides as vectors from $C$, expand $\|u - v\|^2$ by bilinearity, and identify $\langle u, v\rangle$ with $ab\cos\gamma$.
proofs.scope: All triples of points, degenerate ones included. If $A = C$ or $B = C$, then $ab = 0$ and the formula holds for any value of $\cos\gamma$.

roles.why: The inner product gives distances as norms, bilinear expansion and the definition of the angle.

steps.slogan: Translate the three sides into the vectors $u = A - C$ and $v = B - C$.
steps.detail: Distances in a [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) are norms of differences, so $b = \|u\|$, $a = \|v\|$, and $c = \|A - B\| = \|u - v\|$ because $(A - C) - (B - C) = A - B$.

steps.slogan: Expand $\|u - v\|^2$ with the bilinear, symmetric inner product.
steps.detail: Bilinearity and symmetry of the real inner product give $\|u - v\|^2 = \langle u - v, u - v\rangle = \|u\|^2 + \|v\|^2 - 2\langle u, v\rangle$.

steps.slogan: Express $\langle u, v\rangle$ as $\|u\|\,\|v\|\cos\gamma$ through the definition of the angle.
steps.detail: The [angle](c:angle) is $\gamma = \arccos\big(\langle u, v\rangle / (\|u\|\,\|v\|)\big)$, and the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality puts this ratio in $[-1, 1]$, so $\|u\|\,\|v\|\cos\gamma = \langle u, v\rangle$. If $u = 0$ or $v = 0$, both sides are $0$.

steps.slogan: Substitute the side lengths and the inner product into the expansion.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 3 turn $\|u - v\|^2 = \|u\|^2 + \|v\|^2 - 2\langle u, v\rangle$ into $c^2 = b^2 + a^2 - 2ab\cos\gamma$.

concepts.c:euclidean-space: Distances in Euclidean space are norms of difference vectors.
concepts.c:triangle: The three points are the vertices whose sides the formula relates.
concepts.c:angle: The angle is defined through the normalized inner product.
concepts.c:cosine: The cosine of the angle recovers the inner product.
concepts.c:inner-product-space: Bilinearity of the inner product gives the expansion of $\|u - v\|^2$.

proofs.name: Coordinates in the plane of the triangle
proofs.slogan: Place $C$ at the origin and $B$ on the first axis, write $A$ in polar coordinates, and compute $|AB|^2$.
proofs.scope: All triples with $a, b > 0$; if $a = 0$ or $b = 0$ the formula reduces to $c = b$ or $c = a$. The three points lie in a plane with Cartesian coordinates.

roles.why: A Euclidean structure gives orthonormal coordinates in the plane of $A, B, C$ and the distance formula.

steps.slogan: Choose orthonormal coordinates with $C = (0, 0)$ and $B = (a, 0)$.
steps.detail: The points $A, B, C$ lie in a plane of the [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space). Take an orthonormal frame there with origin $C$ and first axis along $CB$, so $B = (a, 0)$.

steps.slogan: Write $A = (b\cos\gamma, b\sin\gamma)$ from its distance and angle at $C$.
steps.detail: The point $A$ has distance $b$ from the origin and makes the [angle](c:angle) $\gamma \in [0, \pi]$ with the positive first axis; a reflection puts it in the upper half-plane. So $A = (b\cos\gamma, b\sin\gamma)$.

steps.slogan: Compute $|AB|^2$ with the distance formula and simplify with $\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1$.
steps.detail: The Pythagorean theorem in coordinates gives $c^2 = (b\cos\gamma - a)^2 + (b\sin\gamma)^2 = b^2(\cos^2\gamma + \sin^2\gamma) - 2ab\cos\gamma + a^2$, which is $a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos\gamma$.

concepts.c:euclidean-space: Euclidean structure gives orthonormal coordinates in the plane of the points.
concepts.c:triangle: The triangle is placed with one vertex at the origin.
concepts.c:angle: The angle at $C$ is the polar angle of $A$.
concepts.c:cosine: The cosine gives the first coordinate of $A$.
concepts.c:inner-product-space: The inner product makes the coordinate frame orthonormal.

source.note: The coordinate proof; Euclid, Elements II.12 and II.13, gives the equivalent proof through the foot of an altitude.

statement: For odd positive integers $a$ and $b$, the [Jacobi symbols](c:jacobi-symbol) satisfy $\left(\frac{a}{b}\right) = (-1)^{\frac{a-1}{2}\cdot\frac{b-1}{2}}\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)$.

hypotheses.text: The integer $a$ is positive and odd.
The integer $b$ is positive and odd.

conclusion: The symbols $\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)$ and $\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)$ agree, except for a sign change when $a \equiv b \equiv 3 \pmod 4$; both are $0$ when $\gcd(a, b) > 1$.

formal.difference: The declaration writes the sign as qrSign b a, the Jacobi symbol of $\chi_4(b)$ modulo $a$, which equals $(-1)^{\frac{a-1}{2}\frac{b-1}{2}}$ for odd $a, b$ (qrSign.neg_one_pow).

proofs.name: Reduction to odd primes by multiplicativity
proofs.slogan: Both sides are completely multiplicative in $a$ and in $b$, so the law follows from quadratic reciprocity for odd primes.
proofs.scope: All odd positive $a, b$, including $a = 1$ or $b = 1$ (empty factorizations, both sides $1$) and pairs with a common factor (both sides $0$).

roles.why: Oddness of $a$ makes $\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)$ defined and lets $a$ factor into odd primes.
Oddness of $b$ makes $\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)$ defined and lets $b$ factor into odd primes.

steps.slogan: Show that both sides are completely multiplicative in $a$ and in $b$.
steps.detail: The symbol $\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)$ is completely multiplicative in $x$ and, as a product of [Legendre symbols](c:legendre-symbol), in odd $y$. The sign $\varepsilon(a, b) = (-1)^{\frac{a-1}{2}\frac{b-1}{2}}$ is symmetric and multiplicative in each odd argument, because $(-1)^{(xy-1)/2} = (-1)^{(x-1)/2}(-1)^{(y-1)/2}$ for odd $x, y$.

steps.slogan: Prove the law for odd primes $a = q$ and $b = p$ by quadratic reciprocity.
steps.detail: For distinct odd [primes](c:prime-number) the Jacobi symbols are Legendre symbols, and quadratic reciprocity gives $\left(\frac{q}{p}\right) = \varepsilon(q, p)\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)$. For $p = q$ both sides are $0$.

steps.slogan: Extend the law from prime $a$ to every odd $a$, for a fixed odd prime $b = p$.
steps.detail: The maps $a \mapsto \left(\frac{a}{p}\right)$ and $a \mapsto \varepsilon(a, p)\left(\frac{p}{a}\right)$ are completely multiplicative on odd $a$, equal $1$ at $a = 1$, and agree at odd primes by step 2. Every odd $a$ is a product of odd primes, so they agree for all odd $a$.

steps.slogan: Extend the law from prime $b$ to every odd $b$ by multiplicativity in $b$.
steps.detail: For fixed odd $a$, the maps $b \mapsto \left(\frac{a}{b}\right)$ and $b \mapsto \varepsilon(a, b)\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)$ are completely multiplicative on odd $b$ and agree at odd primes by step 3. Factoring $b$ into odd primes gives the law for every odd $b$.

concepts.c:jacobi-symbol: The Jacobi symbol is multiplicative in both entries, which drives the reduction.
concepts.c:legendre-symbol: At prime moduli the Jacobi symbol is the Legendre symbol.
concepts.c:prime-number: The law is reduced to the case of two odd primes.

source.note: mathlib writes the right side as a monoid hom ℕ →* ℤ, reduces to primes with jacobiSym.value_at twice, and finishes with legendreSym.quadratic_reciprocity' and qrSign.neg_one_pow.

statement: Let $S$ be an $n \times n$ real or complex [positive-definite matrix](c:positive-definite-matrix). Then $S = L D L^*$, where $L$ is a unit [lower triangular matrix](c:lower-triangular-matrix) and $D$ is a [diagonal matrix](c:diagonal-matrix) with positive diagonal entries.

hypotheses.text: The matrix $S$ is Hermitian and positive definite: $S^* = S$ and $x^* S x > 0$ for every $x \ne 0$.

conclusion: Some unit lower triangular $L$ and positive diagonal $D$ satisfy $S = L D L^*$.

formal.difference: The declaration states the inverse form $D = L^{-1} S (L^{-1})^*$ for the matrix $L^{-1}$ that Gram-Schmidt builds; the form $S = LDL^*$ is LDL.lower_conj_diag. mathlib does not state there that $L$ has unit diagonal or that $D$ is positive.

proofs.name: Gram-Schmidt for the inner product of S
proofs.slogan: Orthogonalize the standard basis for the inner product $y^* S x$; the triangular change of basis conjugates $S$ to a diagonal matrix.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for every size $n$.

roles.why: Positive definiteness makes $y^* S x$ an inner product, so Gram-Schmidt works and the diagonal entries are positive.

steps.slogan: Define the [inner product](c:inner-product-space) $\langle x, y\rangle_S = y^* S x$ on column vectors.
steps.detail: It is linear in $x$, conjugate symmetric because $S^* = S$, and positive definite because $x^* S x > 0$ for $x \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Apply [Gram-Schmidt](c:gram-schmidt) for $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_S$ to the standard basis $e_1, \dots, e_n$.
steps.detail: It gives nonzero, pairwise $S$-orthogonal vectors $u_k = e_k + \sum_{j < k} c_{kj} e_j$. The matrix $W$ with rows $u_k^*$ is therefore unit lower triangular.

steps.slogan: Compute the entries of $W S W^*$ as $S$-inner products of the vectors $u_k$.
steps.detail: The $(k, l)$ entry of $W S W^*$ is $u_k^* S u_l = \langle u_l, u_k\rangle_S$, which is $0$ for $k \ne l$ and $d_k = \langle u_k, u_k\rangle_S > 0$ for $k = l$. So $W S W^* = D$ is diagonal with positive entries.

steps.slogan: Invert the unit lower triangular matrix $W$ to get $S = L D L^*$.
steps.detail: $W$ has determinant $1$, and $L = W^{-1}$ is again unit lower triangular. Multiplying $W S W^* = D$ by $L$ on the left and by $L^*$ on the right gives $S = L D L^*$.

concepts.c:positive-definite-matrix: Positive definiteness turns $S$ into an inner product with positive norms.
concepts.c:lower-triangular-matrix: Gram-Schmidt only mixes earlier basis vectors, so $W$ and $L$ are lower triangular.
concepts.c:diagonal-matrix: Orthogonality of the $u_k$ makes $W S W^*$ diagonal.
concepts.c:inner-product-space: The matrix $S$ defines the inner product in which Gram-Schmidt runs.
concepts.c:gram-schmidt: Gram-Schmidt produces the triangular change of basis.

statement: Let $A$ and $B$ be disjoint nonempty [convex sets](c:convex-set) in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then a [hyperplane](c:hyperplane) separates them: some $v \ne 0$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$ give $\langle a, v\rangle \le c \le \langle b, v\rangle$ for all $a \in A$ and $b \in B$. If $A$ is [compact](c:compact-space) and $B$ is [closed](c:closed-set), both inequalities can be made strict.

hypotheses.text: The sets $A$ and $B$ are convex subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The sets $A$ and $B$ are nonempty.
The sets $A$ and $B$ are disjoint.
For the strict form, $A$ is compact and $B$ is closed.

conclusion: A [separating hyperplane](c:separating-hyperplane) $\{x : \langle x, v\rangle = c\}$ has $A$ and $B$ on opposite closed sides, and on opposite open sides in the strict case.

proofs.name: Nearest point of the difference set
proofs.slogan: Separate $0$ from the convex difference set $B - A$ through a nearest point, and pass to a limit when $0$ lies on its boundary.
proofs.scope: Both forms. The strict form uses a nearest point to $0$ directly; the general form approximates $0$ by points outside the closure of $B - A$.

roles.why: Convexity of $A$ and $B$ makes $B - A$ and its closure convex, which gives the nearest-point inequality and the simplex argument.
Nonempty sets make the difference set nonempty and the bounds $\sup_A$ and $\inf_B$ finite.
Disjointness means $0 \notin B - A$.
A compact set subtracted from a closed set gives a closed set, so $0$ has positive distance from $B - A$.

steps.slogan: Form the difference set $K = B - A$ and check that it is convex without $0$.
steps.detail: The set $K = \{b - a : a \in A, b \in B\}$ is the image of the convex set $B \times A$ under a linear map, so $K$ and its closure $\bar K$ are convex. Since $A \cap B = \emptyset$, $0 \notin K$.

steps.slogan: Separate a point $z$ outside $\bar K$ from $K$ by its nearest point in $\bar K$.
steps.detail: A nearest point $p \in \bar K$ to $z$ exists because closed balls in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are compact. For $w \in K$ and $t \in (0, 1]$, $|p + t(w - p) - z|^2 \ge |p - z|^2$; dividing by $t$ and letting $t \to 0$ gives $\langle w - z, p - z\rangle \ge |p - z|^2 > 0$.

steps.slogan: Take $z = 0$ in the compact and closed case to get strict separation.
steps.detail: If $A$ is compact and $B$ is [closed](c:closed-set), a subsequence argument shows that $K$ is closed, so $0 \notin \bar K$, and step 2 with $v = p$ gives $\langle b, v\rangle - \langle a, v\rangle \ge |v|^2 > 0$. Then $\sup_A \langle a, v\rangle < \inf_B \langle b, v\rangle$, and any $c$ strictly between them works.

steps.slogan: Show that $0$ is not an interior point of the closure $\bar K$.
steps.detail: Otherwise $\bar K$ contains a simplex with $0$ in its interior, whose vertices are limits of points of $K$. Close enough points of $K$ span a simplex that still contains $0$, so convexity gives $0 \in K$, a contradiction.

steps.slogan: Approximate $0$ by points $z_k \notin \bar K$ and pass to a limit of unit normals.
steps.detail: Step 4 gives $z_k \notin \bar K$ with $z_k \to 0$, and step 2 gives unit vectors $v_k$ with $\langle w - z_k, v_k\rangle > 0$ for all $w \in K$. A [subsequence](c:subsequence) of $(v_k)$ converges to a unit vector $v$, and $\langle w, v\rangle \ge 0$ for all $w \in K$.

steps.slogan: Place $c$ between the supremum over $A$ and the infimum over $B$.
steps.detail: Step 5 gives $\langle a, v\rangle \le \langle b, v\rangle$ for all $a \in A$, $b \in B$, so $\sup_A \langle a, v\rangle \le \inf_B \langle b, v\rangle$, both finite as $A$ and $B$ are nonempty. Any $c$ between them separates, and step 3 gives the strict form.

concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity of the difference set drives the nearest-point inequality.
concepts.c:hyperplane: The level set of $\langle \cdot, v\rangle$ at $c$ is the separating hyperplane.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of $A$ makes the difference set closed.
concepts.c:closed-set: A closed difference set keeps $0$ at positive distance.
concepts.c:separating-hyperplane: The conclusion is a hyperplane with the sets on opposite sides.
concepts.c:subsequence: A convergent subsequence of unit normals gives the limiting normal $v$.

source.note: The nearest-point proof, as in Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization (2004), section 2.5.1, with the standard limit argument for sets at distance zero.

statement: Let $p$ be a [nondegenerate critical point](c:nondegenerate-critical-point) of a smooth function $f$ on a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ of dimension $n$, and let $\lambda$ be the number of negative eigenvalues of the [Hessian](c:hessian) at $p$. Then a chart $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ centered at $p$ gives $f = f(p) - x_1^2 - \dots - x_\lambda^2 + x_{\lambda+1}^2 + \dots + x_n^2$ near $p$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f\colon M \to \mathbb{R}$ is smooth on the smooth manifold $M$.
The point $p$ is a [critical point](c:critical-point): the differential of $f$ vanishes at $p$.
The Hessian matrix of $f$ at $p$, in any chart, is invertible.

conclusion: Near $p$, $f$ is $f(p)$ plus a sum of $n$ signed squares of coordinates, with exactly $\lambda$ minus signs.

proofs.name: Hadamard lemma and completing squares
proofs.slogan: Write $f - f(p)$ as a quadratic form with smooth coefficients, then complete the squares one coordinate at a time with the inverse function theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma, in a chart around $p$; for $n = 0$ there is nothing to prove. The count of minus signs comes from Sylvester's law of inertia.

roles.why: Smoothness gives Hadamard's lemma with smooth coefficients and allows the inverse function theorem.
A vanishing differential removes the linear terms, so $f - f(p)$ is quadratic in the coordinates.
An invertible Hessian gives a nonzero pivot after a linear change and fixes the number of negative squares.

steps.slogan: Write $f - f(p) = \sum_{i,j} x_i x_j h_{ij}(x)$ with smooth symmetric $h_{ij}$ by Hadamard's lemma.
steps.detail: In a chart centered at $p$ on a convex neighborhood, $f(x) - f(0) = \sum_i x_i g_i(x)$ with $g_i(x) = \int_0^1 \partial_i f(tx)\,dt$. Since $g_i(0) = \partial_i f(0) = 0$, the same step on each $g_i$ gives $f - f(0) = \sum x_i x_j h_{ij}$, with symmetrized $h_{ij}(0) = \tfrac12 \partial_i\partial_j f(0)$.

steps.slogan: Make the coefficient $H_{rr}(0)$ nonzero by a linear change of the remaining coordinates.
steps.detail: Assume $f - f(0) = \pm u_1^2 \pm \dots \pm u_{r-1}^2 + \sum_{i,j \ge r} u_i u_j H_{ij}(u)$. The block $(H_{ij}(0))_{i,j \ge r}$ is invertible because the [Hessian](c:hessian) at $0$ is, so a linear change of $u_r, \dots, u_n$ gives $H_{rr}(0) \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Complete the square in $u_r$ and check by the inverse function theorem that the result is a chart.
steps.detail: Near $0$ put $v_r = \sqrt{|H_{rr}|}\,\big(u_r + \sum_{i > r} u_i H_{ir}/H_{rr}\big)$ and $v_i = u_i$ for $i \ne r$. Then $f - f(0) = \pm v_1^2 \pm \dots \pm v_r^2 + \sum_{i,j > r} v_i v_j H'_{ij}(v)$, and the Jacobian of $u \mapsto v$ at $0$ is invertible, so $v$ is a chart near $0$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the square completion for $r = 1, \dots, n$ to reach signed squares.
steps.detail: Each step adds one square and keeps smooth coefficients on a smaller neighborhood. After $n$ steps $f = f(p) + \sum_i \pm x_i^2$, and a reordering puts the minus signs first.

steps.slogan: Count the minus signs with Sylvester's law of inertia.
steps.detail: In the final chart the Hessian at $p$ is $\mathrm{diag}(\pm 2)$. At a critical point a change of chart changes the Hessian by a congruence $J^T H J$, and Sylvester's law keeps the number of negative eigenvalues, so there are exactly $\lambda$ minus signs.

concepts.c:nondegenerate-critical-point: Nondegeneracy supplies a nonzero pivot at every completion step.
concepts.c:smooth-manifold: Charts of the manifold reduce the lemma to a neighborhood in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
concepts.c:hessian: The Hessian is the matrix of the quadratic form being diagonalized.
concepts.c:critical-point: At a critical point the linear terms vanish.

source.note: The completing-squares proof of J. Milnor, Morse Theory (1963), Lemma 2.2.

statement: Let $f\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ be a continuous, [square integrable](c:square-integrable-function) [band-limited signal](c:band-limited-signal): its [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) $\hat f(\xi) = \int f(t) e^{-2\pi i \xi t}\,dt$ vanishes outside $[-B, B]$, with $B > 0$. Then $f(t) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} f\big(\tfrac{n}{2B}\big)\,\mathrm{sinc}(2Bt - n)$ for every $t$, where $\mathrm{sinc}(x) = \frac{\sin \pi x}{\pi x}$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is continuous and square integrable on $\mathbb{R}$.
Its Fourier transform vanishes outside $[-B, B]$ for some $B > 0$.

conclusion: The samples $f(n/2B)$ determine $f$ through the [sinc function](c:sinc-function) series, which converges uniformly on $\mathbb{R}$.

proofs.name: Fourier series of the spectrum
proofs.slogan: Expand $\hat f$ on $[-B, B]$ in a Fourier series whose coefficients are the samples, then invert the Fourier transform term by term.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for continuous square-integrable $f$. Uniqueness follows: two such signals with the same samples have the same series.

roles.why: Square integrability puts $\hat f$ in $L^2$, and continuity makes the inversion formula hold at every point.
The support condition makes $\hat f$ a function on the period $[-B, B]$ and shortens the inversion integral to it.

steps.slogan: Write $f(t) = \int_{-B}^{B} \hat f(\xi) e^{2\pi i \xi t}\,d\xi$ by Fourier inversion.
steps.detail: Plancherel gives $\hat f \in L^2$, and it vanishes outside $[-B, B]$, so $\hat f \in L^1$ and the inversion integral is a continuous function equal to $f$ almost everywhere. Both are continuous, so they agree at every $t$.

steps.slogan: Expand $\hat f$ in the [orthonormal basis](c:orthonormal-basis) $e^{-2\pi i n \xi/(2B)}/\sqrt{2B}$ of $L^2[-B, B]$.
steps.detail: By step 1 the [Fourier series](c:fourier-series) coefficients are $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2B}}\int_{-B}^{B} \hat f(\xi) e^{2\pi i n \xi/(2B)}\,d\xi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2B}} f\big(\tfrac{n}{2B}\big)$. So $\hat f = \frac{1}{2B}\sum_n f\big(\tfrac{n}{2B}\big) e^{-2\pi i n \xi/(2B)}$ in $L^2[-B, B]$.

steps.slogan: Integrate the series against $e^{2\pi i \xi t}$ over $[-B, B]$ term by term.
steps.detail: By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, $g \mapsto \int_{-B}^{B} g(\xi) e^{2\pi i \xi t}\,d\xi$ is bounded on $L^2[-B, B]$ with norm $\sqrt{2B}$ for every $t$. So the $L^2$ convergence of step 2 gives uniform convergence in $t$ of the integrated partial sums.

steps.slogan: Evaluate each integrated term as a shifted [sinc function](c:sinc-function).
steps.detail: $\frac{1}{2B}\int_{-B}^{B} e^{2\pi i \xi (t - n/(2B))}\,d\xi = \frac{\sin(\pi(2Bt - n))}{\pi(2Bt - n)} = \mathrm{sinc}(2Bt - n)$. With step 1 this gives $f(t) = \sum_n f\big(\tfrac{n}{2B}\big)\,\mathrm{sinc}(2Bt - n)$, uniformly in $t$.

concepts.c:square-integrable-function: Square integrability puts the spectrum in $L^2$, where Fourier series converge.
concepts.c:band-limited-signal: Band limitation lets one period $[-B, B]$ carry the whole spectrum.
concepts.c:fourier-transform: The spectrum $\hat f$ is expanded and then transformed back.
concepts.c:sinc-function: Each sample contributes a shifted sinc after inversion.
concepts.c:orthonormal-basis: Exponentials on $[-B, B]$ form the basis whose coefficients are samples.
concepts.c:fourier-series: The Fourier series of $\hat f$ has the samples as coefficients.

source.note: Shannon's Fourier-series proof: C. E. Shannon, Communication in the presence of noise, Proceedings of the IRE 37 (1949), 10-21.

statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be [Banach spaces](c:banach-space) and let $T\colon X \to Y$ be a surjective [bounded linear operator](c:bounded-linear-operator). Then $T$ is an [open map](c:open-map): the image of every open subset of $X$ is open in $Y$.

hypotheses.text: The normed spaces $X$ and $Y$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ are complete.
The map $T$ is linear and bounded.
The map $T$ is a [surjection](c:surjection).

conclusion: For every open $U \subseteq X$, the set $T(U)$ is open in $Y$.

formal.difference: The declaration covers continuous semilinear maps between Banach spaces over nontrivially normed fields, for an isometric pair of inverse ring homomorphisms, which includes real and complex bounded operators.

proofs.name: Baire category and successive approximation
proofs.slogan: Baire category puts a ball inside the closure of the image of a ball, successive corrections remove the closure, and translation gives openness.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Completeness of $Y$ enters through Baire category, and completeness of $X$ through the convergent correction series.

roles.why: Completeness of $Y$ gives Baire category, and completeness of $X$ makes the correction series converge.
Linearity moves balls by translation and scaling, and continuity lets $T$ pass through the convergent series.
Surjectivity makes the images of the balls $nB_X$ cover $Y$.

steps.slogan: Find a ball inside the closure of $T(nB_X)$ for some $n$ by Baire category.
steps.detail: With $B_X$ the open unit ball, surjectivity gives $Y = \bigcup_n \overline{T(nB_X)}$, a countable union of closed sets. Since $Y$ is complete, Baire's theorem gives an $n$ for which $\overline{T(nB_X)}$ contains a ball $B(y_0, \varepsilon)$.

steps.slogan: Turn the ball into approximate preimages with a norm bound.
steps.detail: By linearity and symmetry, $\overline{T(2nB_X)} \supseteq B(y_0, \varepsilon) - B(y_0, \varepsilon) \supseteq B(0, \varepsilon)$. Scaling gives $C > 0$ such that every $y \in Y$ has some $x$ with $\|x\| \le C\|y\|$ and $\|y - Tx\| \le \tfrac12\|y\|$.

steps.slogan: Correct the residual repeatedly and sum the corrections in the complete space $X$.
steps.detail: Applying step 2 to $y$, then to the residual $y - Tx_0$, and so on gives $x_k$ with $\|x_k\| \le C 2^{-k}\|y\|$ and residuals at most $2^{-k-1}\|y\|$. The series $x = \sum_k x_k$ converges in the [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X$, $\|x\| \le 2C\|y\|$, and continuity of $T$ gives $Tx = y$.

steps.slogan: Translate the exact preimages to show that $T(U)$ contains a ball around each of its points.
steps.detail: Let $x \in U$ with $B(x, \varepsilon) \subseteq U$. For $\|z - Tx\| < \varepsilon/(2C)$, step 3 gives $w$ with $Tw = z - Tx$ and $\|w\| < \varepsilon$, so $z = T(x + w) \in T(U)$.

concepts.c:banach-space: Completeness gives Baire category in $Y$ and convergent corrections in $X$.
concepts.c:bounded-linear-operator: Linearity and continuity let images of balls scale and series pass through $T$.
concepts.c:open-map: Openness of $T$ is the conclusion, proved ball by ball.
concepts.c:surjection: Surjectivity makes the images of balls cover $Y$.

source.note: mathlib takes $C$ from exists_preimage_norm_le, which sums a geometric series of corrections from exists_approx_preimage_norm_le, which uses Baire category (nonempty_interior_of_iUnion_of_closed); openness is then a translation.

statement: Let $\mu^*$ be an [outer measure](c:outer-measure) on a set $X$, and call $E \subseteq X$ measurable when $\mu^*(A) = \mu^*(A \cap E) + \mu^*(A \setminus E)$ for every $A \subseteq X$. Then the measurable sets form a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) $\mathcal{M}$, and the restriction of $\mu^*$ to $\mathcal{M}$ is a [measure](c:measure).

hypotheses.text: The map $\mu^*\colon \mathcal{P}(X) \to [0, \infty]$ is an outer measure: $\mu^*(\emptyset) = 0$, and $\mu^*$ is monotone and countably subadditive.

conclusion: The Carathéodory-measurable sets form a $\sigma$-algebra on which $\mu^*$ is countably additive.

formal.difference: The declaration only builds the $\sigma$-algebra of Carathéodory-measurable sets, as a Dynkin system closed under intersections. Countable additivity on it is the separate lemma MeasureTheory.OuterMeasure.iUnion_eq_of_caratheodory.

proofs.name: Dynkin system closed under intersections
proofs.slogan: Show that the measurable sets form a Dynkin system closed under intersections, get countable additivity from subadditivity, and conclude by Dynkin's lemma.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Only the inequality $\mu^*(A) \ge \mu^*(A \cap E) + \mu^*(A \setminus E)$ needs proof in each test, since subadditivity gives the reverse.

roles.why: Subadditivity gives the easy inequality in each test, monotonicity compares pieces, and countable subadditivity closes the limit.

steps.slogan: Check that $\emptyset$ is measurable and that complements of measurable sets are measurable.
steps.detail: The test for $E$ is symmetric in $E$ and $X \setminus E$, because $A \cap (X \setminus E) = A \setminus E$. For $E = \emptyset$ it reads $\mu^*(A) = \mu^*(\emptyset) + \mu^*(A)$, which holds as $\mu^*(\emptyset) = 0$.

steps.slogan: Show that the intersection of two measurable sets is measurable.
steps.detail: Testing $A$ with $E$ and then $A \cap E$ with $F$ gives $\mu^*(A) = \mu^*(A \cap E \cap F) + \mu^*((A \cap E) \setminus F) + \mu^*(A \setminus E)$. The last two sets have union $A \setminus (E \cap F)$, so subadditivity gives the test inequality for $E \cap F$.

steps.slogan: Prove $\mu^*(A \cap \bigcup_{i \le n} E_i) = \sum_{i \le n} \mu^*(A \cap E_i)$ for disjoint measurable $E_i$.
steps.detail: Induct on $n$: testing $A \cap \bigcup_{i \le n} E_i$ with the measurable set $E_n$ splits it into $A \cap E_n$ and $A \cap \bigcup_{i < n} E_i$, because the $E_i$ are disjoint.

steps.slogan: Show that a countable disjoint union $E$ of measurable sets is measurable and that $\mu^*$ adds over it.
steps.detail: Finite unions are measurable by steps 1 and 2, so step 3 and monotonicity give $\mu^*(A) \ge \sum_{i \le n} \mu^*(A \cap E_i) + \mu^*(A \setminus E)$ for each $n$. Letting $n \to \infty$ and using countable subadditivity gives the test for $E$, and $A = E$ gives $\mu^*(E) = \sum_i \mu^*(E_i)$.

steps.slogan: Conclude by Dynkin's lemma that the measurable sets form a $\sigma$-algebra carrying a measure.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 4 make the measurable sets a [Dynkin system](c:dynkin-system), and step 2 closes it under finite intersections, so it is a $\sigma$-algebra. Step 4 and $\mu^*(\emptyset) = 0$ make $\mu^*$ a measure on it.

concepts.c:outer-measure: The outer measure supplies subadditivity, the only tool of the proof.
concepts.c:sigma-algebra: The measurable sets are shown to form a sigma-algebra.
concepts.c:measure: Countable additivity on measurable sets makes $\mu^*$ a measure there.
concepts.c:dynkin-system: A Dynkin system closed under intersections is a sigma-algebra.

statement: Let $K$ be a [field](c:field) and $f, g \in K[x]$ [polynomials](c:polynomial) with $g = c\,p_1^{e_1} \cdots p_k^{e_k}$, where $c \ne 0$ and the $p_i$ are distinct monic [irreducible polynomials](c:irreducible-polynomial). Then the [rational function](c:rational-function) $f/g$ equals $q + \sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{e_i} a_{ij}/p_i^{j}$ for one polynomial $q$ and unique polynomials $a_{ij}$ with $\deg a_{ij} < \deg p_i$.

hypotheses.text: The coefficients lie in a field $K$.
The denominator $g \ne 0$ factors as $c\,p_1^{e_1} \cdots p_k^{e_k}$ with $c \in K$ nonzero and distinct monic irreducible $p_i$.

conclusion: $f/g$ has exactly one decomposition into a polynomial part and simple fractions $a_{ij}/p_i^j$ with $\deg a_{ij} < \deg p_i$.

proofs.name: Bezout splitting and division
proofs.slogan: Split off the polynomial part by division, split the proper part over coprime prime powers by Bezout's identity, and expand each piece in powers of $p_i$.
proofs.scope: Existence and uniqueness for every nonzero $g$; for $k = 0$, a constant $g$, the decomposition is $f/g = q$ alone.

roles.why: Over a field, division with remainder works for every nonzero divisor and Bezout's identity holds in $K[x]$.
Distinct monic irreducibles give pairwise coprime prime powers and the primes used in the uniqueness argument.

steps.slogan: Divide $f$ by $g$ to separate a polynomial part from a proper fraction.
steps.detail: [Polynomial division](c:polynomial-division) gives $f = qg + r$ with $\deg r < \deg g$, so $f/g = q + r/g$.

steps.slogan: Split $r/g$ over the coprime factors $p_i^{e_i}$ with Bezout's identity.
steps.detail: Distinct monic irreducibles are coprime, so the [Euclidean algorithm](c:euclidean-algorithm) gives $u, v$ with $u\,p_1^{e_1} + v\,h = 1$, where $h = g/(c\,p_1^{e_1})$, and $r/g = rv/(c\,p_1^{e_1}) + ru/(c\,h)$. Induction on $k$ and division of each numerator write $r/g = P + \sum_i b_i/p_i^{e_i}$ with $P$ a polynomial, which joins $q$, and $\deg b_i < e_i \deg p_i$.

steps.slogan: Expand each numerator $b_i$ in powers of $p_i$ to get the simple fractions.
steps.detail: Repeated division by $p_i$ gives $b_i = \sum_{j=0}^{e_i - 1} c_j p_i^{j}$ with $\deg c_j < \deg p_i$. Then $b_i/p_i^{e_i} = \sum_j c_j/p_i^{e_i - j}$, which has the stated form.

steps.slogan: Show that the difference of two decompositions has all numerators zero.
steps.detail: Write the difference as $0 = q' + \sum b_{ij}/p_i^j$ and let $m$ be the largest $j$ with $b_{1j} \ne 0$. Multiplying by $p_1^m \prod_{i \ge 2} p_i^{e_i}$ leaves only one term not divisible by $p_1$, which forces $p_1 \mid b_{1m}$, impossible as $\deg b_{1m} < \deg p_1$; so every $b_{ij} = 0$ and then $q' = 0$.

steps.slogan: Combine existence from steps 1 to 3 with uniqueness from step 4.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 3 give $f/g = q + \sum_{i,j} a_{ij}/p_i^j$ with $\deg a_{ij} < \deg p_i$. Step 4, applied to the difference of two such decompositions, shows that $q$ and all $a_{ij}$ are unique.

concepts.c:field: Division with remainder and Bezout's identity need field coefficients.
concepts.c:polynomial: Numerators, denominators and the polynomial part are polynomials.
concepts.c:irreducible-polynomial: Irreducible factors are pairwise coprime and act as primes in the uniqueness step.
concepts.c:rational-function: The decomposition rewrites the rational function $f/g$.
concepts.c:polynomial-division: Division separates the polynomial part and expands numerators in powers of $p_i$.
concepts.c:euclidean-algorithm: It produces the Bezout coefficients that split coprime factors.

statement: Let $F$ be a [distribution function](c:distribution-function) with right endpoint $x_F \le \infty$ and excess [conditional distribution](c:conditional-distribution) $F_u(y) = P(X - u \le y \mid X > u)$. Then $F$ lies in the maximum domain of attraction of the extreme value law $H_\xi$ exactly when some positive $\sigma(u)$ gives $\sup_{0 \le y < x_F - u} |F_u(y) - G_{\xi, \sigma(u)}(y)| \to 0$ as $u \uparrow x_F$.

hypotheses.text: The function $F$ is the distribution function of a random variable $X$, with right endpoint $x_F = \sup\{x : F(x) < 1\}$.

The index $\xi$ is real, and $G_{\xi,\sigma}(y) = 1 - (1 + \xi y/\sigma)^{-1/\xi}$ is the [generalized Pareto distribution](c:generalized-pareto-distribution), read as $1 - e^{-y/\sigma}$ for $\xi = 0$.

conclusion: Excesses over a high threshold are uniformly close to a generalized Pareto law exactly for distributions in an extreme value domain of attraction, with the same index $\xi$.

proofs.name: Tail quotient limit
proofs.slogan: Translate the domain of attraction into a limit of tail quotients, read the quotient as the excess distribution, and upgrade pointwise to uniform convergence.
proofs.scope: An outline of both directions. The equivalence of the sequence limit with the continuous tail-quotient limit in step 2 rests on the cited work.

roles.why: The tail $1 - F$ and the endpoint $x_F$ define the excess law and the limit $u \uparrow x_F$.
The index fixes the limit law $H_\xi$ and the matching Pareto law, with $1 - G_{\xi,1} = -\log H_\xi$.

steps.slogan: Rewrite the domain of attraction as a limit of $n(1 - F(a_n x + b_n))$.
steps.detail: Taking logarithms and $\log F \sim F - 1$ near $1$ shows that $F^n(a_n x + b_n) \to H_\xi(x)$ holds exactly when $n(1 - F(a_n x + b_n)) \to (1 + \xi x)^{-1/\xi}$ wherever $1 + \xi x > 0$.

steps.slogan: Replace the sequence index by a continuous threshold $u \uparrow x_F$.
steps.detail: The cited work shows, by monotonicity of $F$ and convergence of types, that the sequence limit holds exactly when $\frac{1 - F(u + x\sigma(u))}{1 - F(u)} \to (1 + \xi x)^{-1/\xi}$ as $u \uparrow x_F$, for some positive $\sigma$. One direction takes $b_n = F^{-1}(1 - 1/n)$ and $a_n = \sigma(b_n)$.

steps.slogan: Read the tail quotient as the rescaled excess distribution.
steps.detail: For $y \ge 0$, $1 - F_u(y) = \frac{1 - F(u + y)}{1 - F(u)}$, so the quotient limit says $F_u(x\sigma(u)) \to G_{\xi,1}(x) = G_{\xi,\sigma(u)}(x\sigma(u))$ for each fixed $x$.

steps.slogan: Upgrade the pointwise limit to a uniform limit with Polya's monotone convergence lemma.
steps.detail: The maps $x \mapsto F_u(x\sigma(u))$ are nondecreasing and converge pointwise to the continuous distribution function $G_{\xi,1}$, so the convergence is [uniform](c:uniform-convergence) in $x$. The substitution $y = x\sigma(u)$ turns this into the stated uniform approximation.

steps.slogan: Reverse the steps to get the domain of attraction from the Pareto approximation.
steps.detail: Uniform approximation gives the tail quotient limit at each $x$ by step 3. The cited equivalence of step 2 and step 1 then give $F^n(a_n x + b_n) \to H_\xi(x)$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two directions into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 4 show that a domain of attraction gives uniform Pareto approximation of the excesses, and step 5 gives the converse, with the same index $\xi$.

concepts.c:distribution-function: The tail $1 - F$ near $x_F$ carries all the information used.
concepts.c:conditional-distribution: The excess law is $X - u$ conditioned on $X > u$.
concepts.c:generalized-pareto-distribution: The Pareto law is the limit of the rescaled excesses.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Uniformity in $y$ is the strong form the theorem asserts.

source.ref: A. A. Balkema and L. de Haan, Residual life time at great age, Annals of Probability 2 (1974), 792-804; J. Pickands III, Statistical inference using extreme order statistics, Annals of Statistics 3 (1975), 119-131
source.note: Balkema and de Haan derive the limit laws of residual life and their domains of attraction; Pickands states the uniform generalized Pareto approximation. The outline follows the textbook route of Embrechts, Klüppelberg and Mikosch, Modelling Extremal Events (1997), section 3.4.

statement: Let $u$ be a real [harmonic function](c:harmonic-function) on the open disk $D = \{|z - c| < R\}$, $R > 0$, continuous on its closure. Then every $w \in D$ satisfies $u(w) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} P_w(\zeta)\,u(\zeta)\,d\theta$, with $\zeta = c + Re^{i\theta}$ and the [Poisson kernel](c:poisson-kernel) $P_w(\zeta) = \frac{R^2 - |w - c|^2}{|\zeta - w|^2}$.

hypotheses.text: The function $u$ is real valued and harmonic on the open disk $D$.
The function $u$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on the closed disk $\bar D$.
The point $w$ lies in the open disk $D$.

conclusion: The value $u(w)$ is the [circle average](c:circle-average) of $P_w u$ over the boundary circle.

formal.difference: The declaration writes the kernel as the real part of the Herglotz-Riesz kernel $\frac{(\zeta - c) + (w - c)}{(\zeta - c) - (w - c)}$, which equals $P_w(\zeta)$ on the circle. The Poisson-kernel form is the companion declaration InnerProductSpace.HarmonicContOnCl.circleAverage_poissonKernel_smul.

proofs.name: Holomorphic completion and a reflected Cauchy integral
proofs.slogan: Write $u$ as the real part of a holomorphic function, prove the formula on smaller circles by Cauchy's formula and a reflected point, then let the radius grow.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with $c = 0$ after a translation. Steps 1 to 4 treat a circle of radius $r < R$; step 5 passes to $r = R$ by continuity.

roles.why: Harmonicity near each smaller closed disk gives a holomorphic $F$ with $u = \mathrm{Re}\,F$.
Continuity on the closed disk makes the circle averages continuous in the radius up to $R$.
With $w$ inside, the kernel stays finite and the reflected point $r^2/\bar w$ lies outside the circle.

steps.slogan: Write $u = \mathrm{Re}\,F$ with $F$ holomorphic near the closed disk of radius $r$.
steps.detail: Take $|w| < r < R$; then $u$ is harmonic on a disk $D(0, r + \delta)$. A harmonic function on a disk has a harmonic conjugate, so $u = \mathrm{Re}\,F$ with $F$ [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) there.

steps.slogan: Express $F(w)$ by the Cauchy integral formula as an average with weight $\zeta/(\zeta - w)$.
steps.detail: For $\zeta = re^{i\theta}$ we have $d\zeta = i\zeta\,d\theta$, so Cauchy's formula reads $F(w) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} F(\zeta)\frac{\zeta}{\zeta - w}\,d\theta$.

steps.slogan: Add a zero integral built from the reflected point $r^2/\bar w$ outside the circle.
steps.detail: The function $F(\zeta)\,\bar w/(r^2 - \bar w\zeta)$ is holomorphic near the closed disk, so Cauchy's theorem gives $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} F(\zeta)\frac{\bar w\zeta}{r^2 - \bar w\zeta}\,d\theta = 0$. On $|\zeta| = r$ the weight equals $\frac{\bar w}{\bar\zeta - \bar w}$.

steps.slogan: Add the two averages and take real parts with the real Poisson kernel.
steps.detail: On the circle, $\frac{\zeta}{\zeta - w} + \frac{\bar w}{\bar\zeta - \bar w} = \frac{r^2 - |w|^2}{|\zeta - w|^2} = \mathrm{Re}\frac{\zeta + w}{\zeta - w}$, a real kernel. So $F(w)$ is the [circle average](c:circle-average) of the kernel times $F$, and real parts give the formula for $u$ at radius $r$.

steps.slogan: Let the radius $r$ increase to $R$ and pass to the limit by continuity.
steps.detail: For $|w| < r < R$, steps 1 to 4 give $u(w)$ as the average of the radius-$r$ kernel times $u$. As $u$ is uniformly [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $\bar D$ and the kernels converge uniformly, these averages are continuous in $r$ up to $R$, so the formula holds at $r = R$.

concepts.c:harmonic-function: A harmonic function is locally the real part of a holomorphic one.
concepts.c:poisson-kernel: The real kernel that remains after the reflection trick is the Poisson kernel.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity up to the boundary lets the radius tend to $R$.
concepts.c:circle-average: Both the Cauchy formula and the result are circle averages.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Cauchy's formula and theorem apply to the holomorphic completion $F$.
